Strike by Hospitality Workers Disrupts Hotel and Restaurant Operations Across Mexican Resorts

A large-scale walkout by hospitality workers has brought significant disruption to hotels and restaurants in major Mexican resort destinations, industry sources confirmed on Wednesday. The industrial action, which began Monday and is ongoing, has forced several prominent resorts and eateries along the Riviera Maya and in Cancún to curtail services, with some venues suspending operations entirely.

Workers affiliated with the National Union of Hospitality and Leisure Employees are demanding a 14% wage increase, improved shift scheduling, and enhanced health benefits. The union claims more than 18,000 staff have joined the strike, affecting hotel reception, housekeeping, food service, and maintenance teams. Picket lines formed outside dozens of hotels and beachfront restaurants, with strikers holding signs reading “Dignity for Hospitality Workers” and “Fair Pay Now.”

According to estimates from the Mexican Hospitality Council, occupancy rates at affected hotels have dropped by as much as 55% since the walkout began. “We’re seeing room cleaning delayed for days, restaurants operating with skeleton crews, and many amenities closed,” said council spokesperson Teresa García. “Our members are doing everything possible to minimize disruption, but the scale of the strike is unprecedented.”

Several hotel chains, including Grupo Sol Caribe and Oceanic Resorts International, have issued statements expressing concern over the impact on guests and urging a resolution. “We respect our employees’ right to organize,” said a spokesperson for Grupo Sol Caribe, “but we are deeply worried about the long-term effects on our reputation if this continues.”

Union leader Jorge Martínez said negotiations with management are ongoing but described talks as “tense.” “We are determined to achieve fair compensation for the people who keep these hotels and restaurants running,” Martínez said at a press conference in Playa del Carmen.

Industry analysts warn that if the strike is prolonged, losses could mount. “The hospitality sector’s recovery from the pandemic was fragile, and this strike puts further pressure on operators’ margins,” said analyst Lucia Herrera at Consultora Turística.

As of Wednesday afternoon, most affected venues remained open but with limited service, and both union and management representatives indicated that no immediate resolution was in sight.
